newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian premier says reforms go on, sees no delay.
newsitem.headline: Serbian premier says reforms go on, sees no delay.

text.p: Serbia is not hesitating or delaying economic reforms but only needs time for a thorough preparation to implement changes, Prime Minister Mirko Marjanovic told Reuters.
A reform law on privatising almost 5,000 firms was presented as a draft late in March.

It has undergone more than two months of public debate involving economists, politicians and businesses, and the ruling Socialists have made changes to the draft. The law is expected to be passed by parliament by mid-July and to become effective late in October.
But Marjanovic insisted there was no delay in implementing privatisation. "There is no delay. We really need several months to prepare," he said.

"We do not want to repeat mistakes which other transition economies have made. This (is) all the more because we partially had a negative experience with ownership transformation," he said in written answers to Reuter questions.

Yugoslavia launched privatisation in the early 1990s but effects of the process were annulled in 1994 after a government decision which left the share of private shareholding capital at barely four percent.
Critics of President Slobodan Milosevic at home and abroad have accused the Serbian Socialists of foot-dragging on reform. But Marjanovic defended the pace of change.
"Because of complexity and political sensitiveness, we think that preparations for the implementation of the law should be adequate and comprehensive," he said.
"Therefore, we are ready to sacrifice a few months for better preparations and enter privatisation uninterruptedly with clear aims and models.
"That is why I think our law will be implemented more successfully compared to other transition economies where weaknesses have come to the surface along with the implementation of the process."

Marjanovic stressed that companies would decide themselves whether to privatise and justified high discounts on the sale prices on the grounds that low-paid workers needed help to become part-owners of companies.

"Our employees with relatively low wages are not able to pay the full price of capital that will be privatised. Therefore it is necessary to secure subsidies for employees when buying socially- and state-owned capital," he said.

Marjanovic said it was realistic for privatisation to begin in the autumn. In the meantime the government would complete data bases with information on companies and future shareholders, and print brochures explaining to companies and workers their rights.

"This year has justly been declared a year of reforms because in 1997 we intend to round up all changes of the economic system and enter the restructuring process," he said. "The ownership transformation aims at clear ownership rights and eventually will increase efficiency of the national economy."
Serbia has already completed a foreign investment law, and a law separating post and telecommunications within PTT Srbije.

The move was a precondition for Serbia to conclude its first major strategic partnership deal with Italian and Greek companies STET and OTE, which recently bought a 49 percent stake in Telekom Srbija for almost $1 billion. -- Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
